In other words, the nonzero vector v is orthogonal to all columns of the matrix  $ M(x) $. Hence the columns of  $ M(x) $ are linearly dependent and  $ Q(x) = 0 $. This argument applies not only to the initial point but also to any other point of the same trajectory. Therefore, if a trajectory lies entirely in a hyperplane, it lies entirely in Z.

(2) By Assumption 2 there exists a point  $ x_*\in K $ such that  $ Q(x_*) \neq 0 $. Hence the polynomial  $ Q $ is not identically zero. A nonzero polynomial vanishes on a set of zero Lebesgue measure, so  $ \lambda(Z) = 0 $. The absolute continuity of the measure  $ \mu $ yields  $ \mu(Z) = 0 $. Since  $ W_\delta\downarrow Z $ as  $ \delta\downarrow 0 $, continuity of measure from above gives  $ \mu(W_\delta)\to\mu(Z)=0 $.
## Step 0: description of the set  $ X_{0} $
Proposition 8 (Step 0). There exists an invariant set of full measure  $ X_0 \subset K $ such that for every  $ x \in X_0 $
$$ \lim_{\delta\rightarrow0}\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{W_{\delta}}(\Phi^{t}x)dt=0. $$
Proof. For each δ > 0, by the Birkhoff–Khinchin theorem [15, 16], for almost every x ∈ K the limit
$$ b_{\delta}(x)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{W_{\delta}}(\Phi^{t}x)dt $$
exists. Here the Birkhoff–Khinchin theorem is applied to the indicator of the neighborhood of Z, i.e., to the function  $ g(x) = \mathbf{1}_{W_\delta}(x) $. Moreover,
$$ \int_{K}b_{\delta}(x)d\mu=\int_{K}\mathbf{1}_{W_{\delta}}(x)d\mu=\mu(W_{\delta}). $$
Since  $ W_\delta $ decreases as  $ \delta \downarrow 0 $, the function  $ \delta \mapsto b_\delta(x) $ is nonincreasing almost everywhere. Define
$$ b_{0}(x)=\lim_{\delta\to0}b_{\delta}(x)=\inf_{\delta>0}b_{\delta}(x). $$
By the monotone convergence theorem,
$$ \int_{K}b_{0}(x)d\mu=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow0}\int_{K}b_{\delta}(x)d\mu=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow0}\mu(W_{\delta})=0, $$
because  $ \mu(W_\delta) \to \mu(Z) = 0 $. Consequently,  $ b_0(x) = 0 $ for  $ \mu $-almost all  $ x $.
$$ X_{0}=\left\{x\in K:\lim_{\delta\rightarrow0}\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{W_{\delta}}(\Phi^{t}x)dt=0\right\}. $$
Then  $ \mu(X_0) = 1 $. The invariance of  $ X_0 $ follows from the invariance of time averages with respect to a shift of the initial moment.

Thus, the set  $ X_0 $ is  $ K $ without the set  $ Z $ and without those points for which the corresponding statement of the Birkhoff–Khinchin ergodic theorem does not hold. For any  $ x \in X_0 $ and any  $ \eta > 0 $ there exists  $ \delta > 0 $ such that
$$ b_{\delta}(x)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{W_{\delta}}(\Phi^{t}x)dt<\eta. $$
